newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy urges Senate to vote for NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy urges Senate to vote for NATO expansion.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to NATO said on Wednesday that Senate rejection of NATO's recent decision to expand was an "intolerable thought" that would do incalculable damage to U.S. credibility.

Envoy Robert Hunter made a strong plea at a State Department conference for an all-out administration effort to sell to the American public the merits of NATO enlargement agreed on July 8 at an alliance summit in Madrid.

The summit invited former Soviet bloc members Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to apply to join the alliance, whose membership has stood at 16 since 1982. The expansion must be ratified by parliaments in all NATO countries.
"The idea of the United States Senate rejecting ratification ... is an intolerable thought," Hunter told an audience of administration officials and experts.
"The consequences, if that were to happen, to the credibility of the United States, not just in NATO but globally, would be I think without calculation," he said.
Addressing the same meeting, NATO Secretary General Javier Solana stressed the importance of the United States within NATO and in the alliance's enlargement process.
"The United States, as leader of the alliance, must continue to lead," Solana said in closing remarks.
This, Solana added, meant that the United States had to be fully engaged in everything the alliance did, not only with troops but also with political support.
He noted that some people thought the Europeans should pick up the burden when NATO-led forces left Bosnia next year and bear the larger share of the cost of an enlarged NATO.

Although many Republicans and Democrats support NATO expansion, some are concerned about financial costs, whether the European allies will pay their share, and whether American troops might one day have to fight in Eastern Europe.

Michael Haltzel, a staff member for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told the conference that European willingness to keep peace-keeping troops in Bosnia after U.S. forces pull out next June could also affect Senate thinking.
Jeremy Rosner, an adviser to President Bill Clinton charged with steering the ratification battle, said that despite the misgivings he expected ultimate success.
"At the end of the day, I am confident that Congress will ratify the addition of these three states to the NATO alliance," he told the conference.
The Senate is expected to take up the issue next spring. A two thirds majority, or 67 of the 100 senators, is required for ratification.
On the cost factor, the administration has estimated that the United States will have to pay a relatively modest $150-200 million per year over 10 years for NATO's expansion.

Hunter argued that this was a bargain compared with an estimated $4 trillion overall that the United States paid to defend Europe during the Cold War, and said it was essential that Congress should approve it.
"Unless the Senate and the House of Representatives are prepared to vote the resources at the time we vote ratification, we can end up with a hollowed-out alliance," he said.
